description: We are ORION, a team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, focused on exploring Earth system trends through data analysis, AI/ML, and visualization. Our team brings together skills in coding, problem-solving, and innovation to develop creative, data-driven solutions for understanding our planet.
summary:
ECHO is an open-source, interactive web app that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar to show how Earth's surface changed over a season, in seven real places on five continents: a monsoon flood in Nepal and India, an avalanche zone, a wildfire, a volcanic eruption, a glacier, a drying lake and a melting ice cap. Optical satellites go blind under monsoon cloud, wildfire smoke and polar night, exactly when the ground is changing. NISAR brings its own microwave light and sees through all of them.

ECHO turns 92 NISAR passes into a map you can play pass by pass, compare side by side, and click for evidence. For every change it shows a full-season timeline, a proposed physical cause from transparent physics rules, and what radar cannot tell us. Every sentence is tagged Measured, Reported or Hypothesis, and anything the rules can't decide stays "uncertain". On the record September 2026 Gandak flood, ECHO measured about 174 km² of open water at the peak, and Sentinel-2 optical images independently support 3 of its 5 flood check points.
details:
ECHO – Project Details

Radar does not photograph the Earth; it listens to how the planet's surface scatters microwave energy.

ECHO translates complex, dual-polarization L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) time-series from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission into an interactive, physics-driven narrative of planetary change.

1. What It Does

ECHO bridges the gap between raw microwave remote sensing and human intuition through two complementary interfaces: Dance (an exploratory spatiotemporal workbench) and Story (a guided scientific narrative).

The Dance Tab — Spatiotemporal SAR Explorer

The Dance view renders an interactive map that sequences every real NISAR orbital pass in chronological order, allowing users to watch landscapes evolve across the season. Users can dynamically toggle between eight analytical layers:

  • HH & HV Radar Backscatter: Co-polarized (HH) and cross-polarized (HV) radiometric brightness showing surface roughness, dielectric shifts, and canopy structure.
  • Open Water: Specular water masks derived from low-backscatter return thresholds.
  • Flooded Vegetation: Inundated canopy and emergent crops isolated via double-bounce scattering signatures.
  • Possible Burn Scar: Post-fire structural canopy loss and surface char zones.
  • Wet (Melting) Snow: Liquid-water phase transitions within the snowpack that absorb L-band energy.
  • Inter-Pass Differential Change: Direct radiometric delta between consecutive orbital passes.
  • Per-Pixel "Dance Card": A synthetic kinematic classification mapping how every individual pixel behaved across the entire annual cycle.

Interactive Analytical Tools:

  • Dual-Date Split Comparison: Swipe interactively between any two acquisition dates to inspect precise spatial boundary shifts.
  • 3D Topographic Drape: Project radar backscatter and change layers onto a 3D digital elevation model to evaluate hydrological flow and slope effects.
  • Regional Trajectory Unfolding: Select any contiguous change polygon to trace its waxing and waning across the full seasonal timeline.
  • Point-Level Telemetry & Export: Click any coordinate on the map to inspect its multi-pass HH/HV backscatter time series and export the raw telemetry as a .csv file.

The Story Tab — Guided Scientific Scrollytelling

The Story view curates location-specific chapters that translate microwave physics into clear, evidence-backed case studies. Each chapter integrates:

  • Before-and-After Swipe Comparisons: High-contrast visual anchors isolating the peak event against baseline conditions.
  • Seasonal Telemetry & Metrics: Quantitative area estimates, backscatter shifts, and duration statistics.
  • Deterministic Causal Attribution: Physics-grounded breakdowns of probable natural and anthropogenic drivers.
  • Multi-Sensor Optical Checkpoints: Side-by-side verification against cloud-free Sentinel-2 optical imagery where available.
  • Epistemic Transparency ("What Radar Cannot Tell Us"): A dedicated breakdown of SAR ambiguities and physical sensor limitations for that specific terrain.

2. How It Works

1. Targeted Data Ingestion

We ingest NISAR Level-2 GCOV (Geocoded Covariance) radar products—specifically dual-polarization HH and HV backscatter—directly from NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility Distributed Active Archive Center (ASF DAAC), performing spatial subsetting on read to extract only our target study footprints.

2. Spatiotemporal Cube & Kinematic Classification

All orbital passes are co-registered and stacked onto a unified spatial grid. Our automated Python processing pipeline then executes a four-stage analysis:

  1. Hydrological Masking: Delineates open water via specular reflection thresholds.
  2. Radiometric Differencing: Computes inter-pass backscatter differentials across both polarizations.
  3. Temporal Signature Classification: Evaluates every pixel's full-season trajectory and classifies its annual "move" into one of five kinematic archetypes: Steady, Pulse (transient anomaly), Step (permanent state shift), Cycle (periodic/phenological oscillation), or Irregular.
  4. Morphological Segmentation: Clusters contiguous changed pixels into discrete, topologically clean vector regions.

3. Deterministic Microwave-Physics Explainer

Rather than relying on an opaque black-box neural network, ECHO employs a deterministic, physics-based inference engine that fuses ESA WorldCover baseline land-cover classes with fundamental radar scattering mechanics:

  • Specular Reflection: Smooth open water acts like a mirror, reflecting incident radar pulses away from the sensor and causing a sharp drop in backscatter.
  • Dihedral Double-Bounce Scattering: When water inundates forests or vertical crop stems, radar pulses bounce off the water surface and hit the trunks before returning directly to the satellite, producing an intense HH brightness spike.
  • Volume Scattering: Dense foliage and agricultural canopies scatter energy in multiple directions, elevating cross-polarized (HV) returns during crop growth and dropping sharply upon harvest or biomass loss.

Based on these mechanisms, the engine proposes physical causes for each polygon—including flooding, water recession, flooded vegetation, crop growth, harvest, or biomass loss.

4. Full-Season Temporal Validation

Pairwise comparisons between just two dates can easily mislead analysts. ECHO validates every region's initial two-date label against its complete seasonal trajectory.

For example, a single-pair brightness increase initially flagged as "crop growth" is automatically audited by the full timeline—revealing that the field actually experienced a rapid hydrological pulse (flooding on 28 September and draining within 12 days).

5. Synoptic Area Synthesis

Landscape processes rarely respect individual polygon boundaries. An Area Synthesis module cross-correlates the temporal timelines of all segmented regions to detect spatially adjacent clusters undergoing synchronized phase transitions.

During the Gandak River flood, our synthesis automatically linked 8 neighbouring regions (304 km²) that inundated and drained in lockstep, coalescing fragmented detections into a single coherent hydrological event.

6. Cloud-Native Visualization & Delivery

Processed rasters and vector syntheses are dynamically tiled and served through a lightweight FastAPI backend powered by rio-tiler, while a responsive, static web frontend built on MapLibre GL JS handles GPU-accelerated map rendering and interactive charting.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

  • All-Weather Public Science & Visual Literacy: Optical satellites are frequently blinded by cloud cover, wildfire smoke, and nightfall right when disasters peak. Because L-band SAR penetrates clouds, smoke, and vegetation canopies, ECHO empowers students and the public to witness the physical footprint of floods, wildfires, and volcanic eruptions even when no clear optical photograph exists.
  • Actionable Decision Support for Disaster Management: Emergency planners, hydrologists, and responders receive immediate, machine-readable outputs—including downloadable GeoJSON change perimeters, point-level CSV backscatter histories, and quantitative flood-extent estimates for critical dates.
  • Autonomous Operational Readiness: Engineered around NISAR's 12-day orbital repeat cycle, the entire deterministic pipeline is designed to trigger automatically whenever a new GCOV scene lands at ASF DAAC—enabling continuous, cloud-proof flood and land-change monitoring anywhere on Earth.

Writing

4. Tools, Languages, and Software

Programming Languages

  • Python 3.12 (scientific pipeline & API)
  • JavaScript ES Modules
  • HTML5
  • CSS3

Scientific & Geospatial Backend

  • NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image (array math & morphological segmentation)
  • h5py, rasterio, rio-tiler (HDF5/COG ingestion & dynamic map tiling)
  • Shapely (vector geometry topology)

API & Web Server

  • FastAPI
  • Uvicorn (asynchronous tile and metadata delivery)

Frontend Visualization

  • MapLibre GL JS (2D/3D WebGL vector and raster rendering)

Testing & Verification

  • pytest (backend pipeline & physics unit tests)
  • Node.js built-in test runner (frontend logic)

Packaging & Cloud Delivery

  • Dockerized microservice architecture
  • Object storage hosted on Cloudflare R2
  • Automated cryptographic checksum verification at container startup

Hardware Footprint

  • Zero GPU dependency.
  • Engineered for extreme efficiency—runs smoothly on a standard consumer laptop or a modest 2 GB RAM cloud instance.

5. How the Project Is Creative

  • Choreographing Radar Physics ("The Season as a Dance"): Multi-pass SAR time series are notoriously difficult for non-specialists to interpret. By translating each pixel's annual backscatter trajectory into an intuitive kinetic archetype (Steady, Pulse, Step, Cycle, Irregular), ECHO turns abstract decibel curves into a readable visual language.
  • Epistemic Self-Correction (Full-Season Verification): Instead of hiding algorithmic edge cases, ECHO uses its full-season timeline to audit its own initial pairwise classifications—openly highlighting moments where longitudinal context overturns a two-date snapshot.
  • Macro-Scale Event Coalescence: By clustering neighboring polygons that share synchronized temporal phase shifts, ECHO moves beyond isolated pixel changes to reconstruct unified, landscape-scale disasters.
  • Tripartite Epistemic Tagging: To combat scientific overreach, every narrative sentence in the platform is explicitly badged as Measured (direct NISAR radiometric observation), Reported (external ground-truth or agency documentation), or Hypothesis (physics-derived causal inference). Users never have to guess where raw data ends and interpretation begins.
  • Unified Multi-Hazard Physics Engine: A single, cohesive framework interprets radar scattering across five distinct Earth-system domains: hydrology, agriculture, wildfire ecology, volcanology, and the cryosphere (snow and ice).

6. Factors Considered During Development

Scientific Honesty & Uncertainty Transparency

  • All derived spatial footprints are explicitly badged as "estimate" rather than absolute ground truth.
  • Ambiguous scattering signatures are transparently labeled "uncertain" rather than forced into a confident category.
  • Zero Synthetic Interpolation: The 27 Jul – 10 Aug 2026 NISAR data outage is rendered honestly as an explicit observational gap in the timeline and is never masked with interpolated or fabricated frames.

Multi-Sensor Scientific Validity

  • NISAR L-band serves strictly as the primary quantitative measurement source across the platform.
  • Sentinel-2 optical imagery is used exclusively as an independent visual checkpoint, never fused to alter radar measurements.
  • Wildfire canopy-loss detections are cross-validated against a second radar frequency (C-band SAR) to confirm structural stripping across wavelengths.

Accounting for Radar Geometry Limitations

  • Steep topographic slopes prone to radar shadow and layover distortions are systematically screened out using digital elevation model (DEM) slope masks before change detection occurs.

Frictionless Accessibility & Open Science

  • Designed for universal reach with plain-language legends, full keyboard navigation shortcuts, a mobile-responsive interface, and zero login or paywall barriers.
  • Built exclusively on free, open-access satellite archives and released as 100% open-source code.
